description: Dominant Welsh kingdom in Snowdonia (c. 500–1283) that repeatedly unified Wales under Rhodri Mawr and Llywelyn ap Gruffudd; its natural mountain fortress resisted Anglo-Norman pressure longer than any other Welsh polity until Edward I's systematic conquest, construction of the Iron Ring castles, and the Statute of Wales (1284) extinguished Welsh independence.

temporal.notes: Dominant Welsh kingdom before Edwardian conquest.

geographic.notes: Centroid approximate; polygon pending schematic or OHM sourcing.

lifecycle_phases.description: Rhodri Mawr unifies north Wales; dynasty at height.
Owain Gwynedd and successors rebuild after Norman raids.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd; English wars culminating in conquest.
Edward I's conquest; Gwynedd absorbed into English crown.

rise_factors.description: Snowdonia provided an almost impregnable mountain refuge; the highland core was never successfully conquered until 1282.
Aberffraw/Venedotian dynasty maintained remarkably long and consistent rule through the 9th–11th centuries.
Welsh guerrilla tactics in mountain terrain negated English heavy cavalry advantages.

The mountains of Snowdonia gave Gwynedd an almost impregnable natural fortress against invasion, allowing Welsh kings to retreat, regroup, and recover from defeats that would have destroyed more exposed kingdoms.
Llywelyn the Great unified most of Wales under Gwynedd's hegemony in the early 13th century, gaining recognition as Prince of Wales and extracting homage from other Welsh rulers.

decline_factors.description: Edward I mounted systematic campaigns 1277–1283, using coastal logistics to bypass the mountains.
Llywelyn ap Gruffudd's death in 1282 without a capable male successor left no legitimate resistance.
English conquest and the Statute of Rhuddlan 1284 imposed English administrative law on Wales.
Edward I's two military campaigns (1277 and 1282–83) conclusively defeated Llywelyn ap Gruffudd and ended Welsh independence, with the Statute of Rhuddlan imposing English law and administration.
Edward's construction of massive concentric castles, Caernarfon, Harlech, Beaumaris, Conwy, created an iron ring of English military power around Gwynedd that no Welsh revolt could break.
